I had surgery in my mid-20s. Big time surgery. Most of my vertebrates were fused together and I could barely walk without a walker. My doctor said the best thing I could do was to exercise every day, so I tried my best and dutifully went for walks--even when it was storming or cold.

Additionally, I was completely broke even with my insurance covering most of my >$200,000 surgery. I wore tattered sweat pants and an equally damaged coat (though the coat was actually half eaten by my dog.) I must have looked homeless with my hair and beard all overgrown.

I was walking, and regretting not wearing more layers because the cold that day was more bitter than I expected, and I had to clutch my clothes to keep the wind from coming in. But I was arrogant and told myself I didn't care.

Anyhow, I'm walking for awhile and I enter this nice neighborhood and there is this Saudi Arabian guy around my age loading up his Lexus.

Now to pause for some background: at this college campus where I was, Saudi guys had a very bad reputation. We had tons of international students (>60%) because it was a tech school that was cheap enough for other countries to afford to outsource to. People from almost all the nations were really cool, laid back, and interested in learning from each other. We all had a diverse pallet of friends... but Saudi's were different. They were known as womanizers, and drove their premium cars through the parking lots so fast and so close (almost hitting us) we all hated them. We also had plenty of experience with them bribing people to do their homework and to up their test grades for them.

Now, back to the story: This Saudi guy sees me and I think nothing of it at first. But he keeps glancing and I just keep walking... but then he starts calling to me.

I get a little nervous, and he proceeds to grab something from his car and walks over to me... and then quite surprisingly, he hands me a coat...

But not just any coat; but an old, authentic camel skin coat. It was worn down but absolutely beautifully crafted. He says, "It's from Saudi Arabia and you cannot find anything like it in the States." It was so heavy... and unimaginably warm. I really cannot stress how warm this thing was because I went from bitter cold to sweating hot within a minute or two.

All he asked in return was to take my picture wearing the coat while making a peace sign.

He thought he was giving me a coat, but really he was giving me the most humbling lesson about generalizing people that I could ever get. I still have that coat, and it ranks as one of the most sentimental possessions of my life.

North American Arms 22 Mag Mini revolver

I recently picked up one of their 'Earl' revolvers with a 3" barrel, like this one:

http://northamericanarms.com/firearms/earl/1860-3c.html

It was kind of an impulse purchase but I've really enjoyed fooling with it. I've since replaced the big wooden grips with the small slip-on rubber boot grip.

http://i.imgur.com/2LMdSGt.jpg

There are three tricks to these things. One, put the hammer on half cock before removing the cylinder, and cradle the cylinder with your fingers before you pull that central pin, or it will fall right out. Two, tiny guns like this (and I include the Ruger Bearcat here) demand a rock solid grip, and they will educate you about that if you're doing it wrong. When that hammer falls, everything wants to move. Three, shoot the gun from a sitting position, where you have plenty of room to have your stuff spread out around you and you're in no particular hurry. That's when it's the most fun, and you won't mind the reloading process at all.

I tend to sit down with the thing expecting to just shoot five or ten rounds, and end up shooting the whole box. I find I just get absorbed with it, in a way that doesn't happen with other guns, and I like that. I usually run CCI Long CB caps, which are accurate at the ranges I'll attempt, which is currently limited to fifty feet or so max. Most of my shooting is at things like bumblebees and thistle tops at ten feet or so, which is safe with CB caps but more hazardous with the more powerful ammunition.

My gun won't shoot to point of aim but I've learned to compensate by adjusting the sight picture. That's the only defect I've found; its otherwise a well-designed and well-crafted arm. From seated position I can knock over a soda can at fifty feet about half the time, and I'm still learning. When I carry it, it rides in a leather knife sheath that happens to fit almost perfectly.
